extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism students, media practitioners and fellows interested in constructive/solutions-focused reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and reflective criteria for producing constructive (solutions-focused) journalism: principles, stance, form, methods and audience engagement to make reporting constructive. Emphasis on practical processes learned during a fellowship and how to adapt them to contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three pillars: finding solutions, truth and community
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive Journalism rests on three pillars; finding solutions, truth and community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These pillars underpin the whole approach: stories should seek constructive responses or solutions, remain truthful and accurate, and engage or build community. The reflection emphasizes that these are not abstract ideals but actionable aims with accompanying processes and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curious, non-judgemental stance
rubrics_metrics.description: The journalist is encouraged to be curious, not judgemental or dramatic, exploring nuance, and inviting audiences into conversations about the process of knowledge gathering and creating collaborative outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sensational or purely judgmental tones; foreground genuine inquiry and nuance. This stance helps invite reader participation and positions the report as exploratory rather than declarative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitative journalist role: maintain authority without condescension
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of being a judge, jury and executioner, the journalist facilitates understanding; written from the view of a collaborative journalist, who has and maintains their authority, but does not use it to separate themselves from readers or the audience, and condescend them from an ivory tower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance is required: keep professional authority (fact-checking, verification, expertise) while avoiding distancing language or patronizing presentation. The journalist should enable readers' understanding and involvement rather than simply delivering verdicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal constructive intent early (introduction & form)
rubrics_metrics.description: A large portion of constructive stories can be identified by the written content and form of the introduction, in part, the intention of the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on tacked-on solutions at the end. Make the purpose/intention of being constructive visible in the introduction and through structural choices so audiences can recognize the piece's constructive aims from the outset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular interaction with community (invite participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive Journalism aims to be circular in its interaction with its community of readers and contributors, inviting audiences into conversations about the process of knowledge gathering and creating collaborative outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reporting to enable ongoing dialogue and contribution from readers/contributors. Use structures that allow feedback, co-creation and iterative development of solutions rather than one-way publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be open-ended and frank about uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism also aims to be open ended in its reporting generally; being frank when we don’t have a solution or finality for an issue and guiding readers through this uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly acknowledge unknowns and the limits of current knowledge; guide readers through complexity rather than pretending certainty. Openness about absence of final answers is itself part of constructiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and precision while accepting uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive Journalism aims to be as clear and precise as possible, but it is also comfortable with uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for clear, precise communication of facts, processes and options even while explaining ambiguities and provisional findings. Clarity helps readers engage with complex or unresolved problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use constructive language and frameworks to shape form
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of Constructive Journalism itself provides a framework to guide the journalist in creating a form that embodies its content, helping make the story constructive by terming, describing its structure and form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the specific vocabulary and conceptual frameworks of constructive journalism to influence story architecture (angles, sections, signposting) so form and intent align. Terminology can act as a design tool for constructiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical methods for finding and reporting solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are processes to achieve constructive aims that are fairly comprehensive and understandable, such as the method of finding and developing how you may report solutions to a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply concrete methodologies (research, solution identification, vetting, presenting trade-offs) rather than treating constructiveness as mere ideology. The fellowship provided toolkits and practical approaches to implement solution-focused reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain critical rigor and correctability from traditional journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Good quality traditional journalism offers nuance, is critical and is correctable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive journalism should augment rather than replace traditional journalistic values: continue to be critical, fact-based and open to correction. Avoid equating constructiveness with softness or abandoning investigative scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventiveness and multi-format storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: What is needed is inventiveness, creating places for work that disturbs, excites and challenges. Not just long form, but many layered multiforms that are rich enough for audiences to continue to explore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use varied formats (visual stories, freelancing-focused pieces, multi-layered multimedia) to build depth and sustain audience exploration. Be experimental in form to match the complexity of solutions and community needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt constructiveness to niche/topic and organizational constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive processes are being created for different niches, not strictly journalism... In Australia, most journalists in mainstream media are budget and time constrained; there is very little accommodation for the audience-driven or solutions-driven forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor constructive methods to the issue, audience and newsroom realities (time, budget, ownership). Recognize structural barriers (media concentration, editorial agendas) and adapt feasible practices accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposeful reporting: make readers smarter, not just informed
rubrics_metrics.description: The ease of identifying, as well as reading, a constructive piece of journalism from the audience’s point of view makes Constructive Journalism more valuable when you can signal to the reader that you intend to make them smarter, rather than just more informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design pieces with clear educative aims—help readers understand systems, trade-offs and options. Make the purpose evident in form so reader and content are held together and engagement is deeper and ongoing.
